With significant expansion on the demand and supply side, including behind-the-meter generation or energy storage capabilities to come, along with dynamic workloads, it is important to view this challenge from the lens of grid reliability. There is a clear need to put together a framework to specify ramp rates, acceptable oscillations, and allowable protection schemes, etc., that would assist in sustaining reliable grid operation and not exacerbate grid outage risks. This necessitates the need for power system studies that can model grid and data center dynamics/interactions in a unified framework. To enable the study of data center and grid interactions, a high-fidelity power system model of the data center needs to be developed, particularly one that can cater to the fast-timescale needs of dynamic AI loads and fast-timescale grid instability events (such as those reported in the NERC incident review [NERC 2025]). Two types of modeling frameworks are necessary to evaluate the impacts of data centers on grid stability: 1. Offline electromagnetic transient (EMT) domain simulations (Badrzadeh n.d.) (using tools such as PSCAD and EMTP) of the data center power system with appropriate representations of the grid 2. Real-time EMT domain simulations (in a controller-hardware-in-the-loop [CHIL] framework [IEEE 2025]) with the inclusion of the data center and grid-side controls. In this regard, a technical report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies performed EMT domain CHIL simulations for the 70-MW data center design of Verrus (Vaidhynathan et al. 2025). 2 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Design/Operational Philosophy of Data Centers Data center designs are entirely focused on providing a high uptime for computing/information technology (IT) (Uptime Institute n.d.) and void any consideration for demand flexibility and grid resilience. A typical data center uptime requirement can range from 99% to 99.999% (leading to appropriate tier categories) (Uptime Institute n.d.), presenting a very short window of acceptable downtime, outside of which means significant losses for businesses.
